content.text:
Sources I found:
- Angular guide: "Signals"[^ng-signals-overview]
- Angular guide: "RxJS interop with signals"[^ng-signals-rxjs]

What Angular signals are
- Signals are a built-in reactivity primitive in Angular for representing values that change over time. A signal holds a value and notifies dependents automatically when that value changes, so code that reads the signal re-evaluates/reacts without manual subscription management[^ng-signals-overview].
- There are a few related primitives: writable signals (you can set their value), computed signals (derive a value from other signals), and effects (run imperative code in response to signal changes) — together these let you express reactive data flow in the app[^ng-signals-overview].

How they behave (short)
- Reading a signal registers a dependency; when the signal is updated, Angular re-runs computed signals and effects that depend on it.
- Signals are synchronous by default: updates propagate immediately to dependents.
- Signals interoperate with existing RxJS Observables via helpers like toSignal() and toObservable() to convert between the two forms of reactivity[^ng-signals-rxjs].

When to use signals
- Use signals when you want simpler, explicit local state and reactive derivations without the boilerplate of subscriptions and change-detection hacks. They reduce the need to manually manage subscriptions, Subjects, or manual change detection for many common patterns[^ng-signals-overview].
- Prefer signals for component-local state or derived view-model values where synchronous, fine-grained reactivity is helpful (e.g., computed values used by the template).
- Use computed signals to encapsulate derived logic instead of recomputing in templates or in getters that trigger extra change detection work.
- Use effects for side effects that should run in response to signal changes (e.g., logging, imperatively updating non-Angular APIs).
- When you already use RxJS streams across many layers, continue using Observables; convert when needed. Signals are complementary to RxJS — use toSignal/toObservable when bridging between the two models rather than rewriting everything at once[^ng-signals-rxjs][^ng-signals-overview].

Concise recommendation
- Adopt signals for component and local state that benefits from direct, synchronous dependency tracking and simpler code (computed values + effects).
- Keep using Observables where their stream semantics (time, cancellation, complex operators) are required, and bridge between the two when appropriate[^ng-signals-overview][^ng-signals-rxjs].

content.text:
Sources I found:
- Angular guide: "Signals"[^ng-signals-overview]
- Angular guide: "RxJS interop with signals"[^ng-signals-rxjs]

What Angular signals are
- Signals are a built-in reactivity primitive in Angular for representing values that change over time. A signal holds a value and notifies dependents automatically when that value changes, so code that reads the signal re-evaluates/reacts without manual subscription management[^ng-signals-overview].
- There are a few related primitives: writable signals (you can set their value), computed signals (derive a value from other signals), and effects (run imperative code in response to signal changes) — together these let you express reactive data flow in the app[^ng-signals-overview].

How they behave (short)
- Reading a signal registers a dependency; when the signal is updated, Angular re-runs computed signals and effects that depend on it.
- Signals are synchronous by default: updates propagate immediately to dependents.
- Signals interoperate with existing RxJS Observables via helpers like toSignal() and toObservable() to convert between the two forms of reactivity[^ng-signals-rxjs].

When to use signals
- Use signals when you want simpler, explicit local state and reactive derivations without the boilerplate of subscriptions and change-detection hacks. They reduce the need to manually manage subscriptions, Subjects, or manual change detection for many common patterns[^ng-signals-overview].
- Prefer signals for component-local state or derived view-model values where synchronous, fine-grained reactivity is helpful (e.g., computed values used by the template).
- Use computed signals to encapsulate derived logic instead of recomputing in templates or in getters that trigger extra change detection work.
- Use effects for side effects that should run in response to signal changes (e.g., logging, imperatively updating non-Angular APIs).
- When you already use RxJS streams across many layers, continue using Observables; convert when needed. Signals are complementary to RxJS — use toSignal/toObservable when bridging between the two models rather than rewriting everything at once[^ng-signals-rxjs][^ng-signals-overview].

Concise recommendation
- Adopt signals for component and local state that benefits from direct, synchronous dependency tracking and simpler code (computed values + effects).
- Keep using Observables where their stream semantics (time, cancellation, complex operators) are required, and bridge between the two when appropriate[^ng-signals-overview][^ng-signals-rxjs].

content.text:
Sources: Angular Signals guide[^ng-signals-overview] and RxJS interop[^ng-signals-rxjs].

What they are
- Signals are Angular’s built-in reactive primitive that hold a value and automatically notify dependents when the value changes (writable signals, computed signals, and effects). They remove manual subscription management and enable synchronous dependency tracking[^ng-signals-overview].

When to use them
- Use signals for component-local state and computed view-model values to simplify code and avoid manual subscriptions.
- Use computed signals for derived values and effects for side effects triggered by changes.
- Keep using Observables when you need stream semantics (operators, cancellation); bridge with toSignal()/toObservable() when needed[^ng-signals-overview][^ng-signals-rxjs].

Want a one-line code example for each (writable, computed, Observable→signal)?

content.text:
Sources I found:
- Angular guide: "Signals"[^ng-signals-overview]
- Angular guide: "RxJS interop with signals"[^ng-signals-rxjs]

What Angular signals are
- Signals are a built-in reactivity primitive in Angular for representing values that change over time. A signal holds a value and notifies dependents automatically when that value changes, so code that reads the signal re-evaluates/reacts without manual subscription management[^ng-signals-overview].
- There are a few related primitives: writable signals (you can set their value), computed signals (derive a value from other signals), and effects (run imperative code in response to signal changes) — together these let you express reactive data flow in the app[^ng-signals-overview].

How they behave (short)
- Reading a signal registers a dependency; when the signal is updated, Angular re-runs computed signals and effects that depend on it.
- Signals are synchronous by default: updates propagate immediately to dependents.
- Signals interoperate with existing RxJS Observables via helpers like toSignal() and toObservable() to convert between the two forms of reactivity[^ng-signals-rxjs].

When to use signals
- Use signals when you want simpler, explicit local state and reactive derivations without the boilerplate of subscriptions and change-detection hacks. They reduce the need to manually manage subscriptions, Subjects, or manual change detection for many common patterns[^ng-signals-overview].
- Prefer signals for component-local state or derived view-model values where synchronous, fine-grained reactivity is helpful (e.g., computed values used by the template).
- Use computed signals to encapsulate derived logic instead of recomputing in templates or in getters that trigger extra change detection work.
- Use effects for side effects that should run in response to signal changes (e.g., logging, imperatively updating non-Angular APIs).
- When you already use RxJS streams across many layers, continue using Observables; convert when needed. Signals are complementary to RxJS — use toSignal/toObservable when bridging between the two models rather than rewriting everything at once[^ng-signals-rxjs][^ng-signals-overview].

Concise recommendation
- Adopt signals for component and local state that benefits from direct, synchronous dependency tracking and simpler code (computed values + effects).
- Keep using Observables where their stream semantics (time, cancellation, complex operators) are required, and bridge between the two when appropriate[^ng-signals-overview][^ng-signals-rxjs].

Would you like short examples showing a writable signal, a computed signal, and converting an Observable to a signal?

content.text:
Sources I found:
- Angular guide: "Signals"[^ng-signals-overview]
- Angular guide: "RxJS interop with signals"[^ng-signals-rxjs]

What Angular signals are
- Signals are a built-in reactivity primitive in Angular for representing values that change over time. A signal holds a value and notifies dependents automatically when that value changes, so code that reads the signal re-evaluates/reacts without manual subscription management[^ng-signals-overview].
- There are a few related primitives: writable signals (you can set their value), computed signals (derive a value from other signals), and effects (run imperative code in response to signal changes) — together these let you express reactive data flow in the app[^ng-signals-overview].

How they behave (short)
- Reading a signal registers a dependency; when the signal is updated, Angular re-runs computed signals and effects that depend on it.
- Signals are synchronous by default: updates propagate immediately to dependents.
- Signals interoperate with existing RxJS Observables via helpers like toSignal() and toObservable() to convert between the two forms of reactivity[^ng-signals-rxjs].

When to use signals
- Use signals when you want simpler, explicit local state and reactive derivations without the boilerplate of subscriptions and change-detection hacks. They reduce the need to manually manage subscriptions, Subjects, or manual change detection for many common patterns[^ng-signals-overview].
- Prefer signals for component-local state or derived view-model values where synchronous, fine-grained reactivity is helpful (e.g., computed values used by the template).
- Use computed signals to encapsulate derived logic instead of recomputing in templates or in getters that trigger extra change detection work.
- Use effects for side effects that should run in response to signal changes (e.g., logging, imperatively updating non-Angular APIs).
- When you already use RxJS streams across many layers, continue using Observables; convert when needed. Signals are complementary to RxJS — use toSignal/toObservable when bridging between the two models rather than rewriting everything at once[^ng-signals-rxjs][^ng-signals-overview].

Concise recommendation
- Adopt signals for component and local state that benefits from direct, synchronous dependency tracking and simpler code (computed values + effects).
- Keep using Observables where their stream semantics (time, cancellation, complex operators) are required, and bridge between the two when appropriate[^ng-signals-overview][^ng-signals-rxjs].

content.text:
Sources I found:
- Angular guide: "Signals"[^ng-signals-overview]
- Angular guide: "RxJS interop with signals"[^ng-signals-rxjs]

What Angular signals are
- Signals are a built-in reactivity primitive in Angular for representing values that change over time. A signal holds a value and notifies dependents automatically when that value changes, so code that reads the signal re-evaluates/reacts without manual subscription management[^ng-signals-overview].
- There are a few related primitives: writable signals (you can set their value), computed signals (derive a value from other signals), and effects (run imperative code in response to signal changes) — together these let you express reactive data flow in the app[^ng-signals-overview].

How they behave (short)
- Reading a signal registers a dependency; when the signal is updated, Angular re-runs computed signals and effects that depend on it.
- Signals are synchronous by default: updates propagate immediately to dependents.
- Signals interoperate with existing RxJS Observables via helpers like toSignal() and toObservable() to convert between the two forms of reactivity[^ng-signals-rxjs].

When to use signals
- Use signals when you want simpler, explicit local state and reactive derivations without the boilerplate of subscriptions and change-detection hacks. They reduce the need to manually manage subscriptions, Subjects, or manual change detection for many common patterns[^ng-signals-overview].
- Prefer signals for component-local state or derived view-model values where synchronous, fine-grained reactivity is helpful (e.g., computed values used by the template).
- Use computed signals to encapsulate derived logic instead of recomputing in templates or in getters that trigger extra change detection work.
- Use effects for side effects that should run in response to signal changes (e.g., logging, imperatively updating non-Angular APIs).
- When you already use RxJS streams across many layers, continue using Observables; convert when needed. Signals are complementary to RxJS — use toSignal/toObservable when bridging between the two models rather than rewriting everything at once[^ng-signals-rxjs][^ng-signals-overview].

Concise recommendation
- Adopt signals for component and local state that benefits from direct, synchronous dependency tracking and simpler code (computed values + effects).
- Keep using Observables where their stream semantics (time, cancellation, complex operators) are required, and bridge between the two when appropriate[^ng-signals-overview][^ng-signals-rxjs].

Would you like short examples showing a writable signal, a computed signal, and converting an Observable to a signal?

- Signals are a built-in reactivity primitive in Angular for representing values that change over time. - Reading a signal registers a dependency; when the signal is updated, Angular re-runs computed signals and effects that depend on it.

content.text:
Sources I found:
- Angular guide: "Signals"[^ng-signals-overview]
- Angular guide: "RxJS interop with signals"[^ng-signals-rxjs]

What Angular signals are
- Signals are a built-in reactivity primitive in Angular for representing values that change over time. A signal holds a value and notifies dependents automatically when that value changes, so code that reads the signal re-evaluates/reacts without manual subscription management[^ng-signals-overview].
- There are a few related primitives: writable signals (you can set their value), computed signals (derive a value from other signals), and effects (run imperative code in response to signal changes) — together these let you express reactive data flow in the app[^ng-signals-overview].

How they behave (short)
- Reading a signal registers a dependency; when the signal is updated, Angular re-runs computed signals and effects that depend on it.
- Signals are synchronous by default: updates propagate immediately to dependents.
- Signals interoperate with existing RxJS Observables via helpers like toSignal() and toObservable() to convert between the two forms of reactivity[^ng-signals-rxjs].

When to use signals
- Use signals when you want simpler, explicit local state and reactive derivations without the boilerplate of subscriptions and change-detection hacks. They reduce the need to manually manage subscriptions, Subjects, or manual change detection for many common patterns[^ng-signals-overview].
- Prefer signals for component-local state or derived view-model values where synchronous, fine-grained reactivity is helpful (e.g., computed values used by the template).
- Use computed signals to encapsulate derived logic instead of recomputing in templates or in getters that trigger extra change detection work.
- Use effects for side effects that should run in response to signal changes (e.g., logging, imperatively updating non-Angular APIs).
- When you already use RxJS streams across many layers, continue using Observables; convert when needed. Signals are complementary to RxJS — use toSignal/toObservable when bridging between the two models rather than rewriting everything at once[^ng-signals-rxjs][^ng-signals-overview].

Concise recommendation
- Adopt signals for component and local state that benefits from direct, synchronous dependency tracking and simpler code (computed values + effects).
- Keep using Observables where their stream semantics (time, cancellation, complex operators) are required, and bridge between the two when appropriate[^ng-signals-overview][^ng-signals-rxjs].

content.text:
Sources I found:
- Angular guide: "Signals"[^ng-signals-overview]
- Angular guide: "RxJS interop with signals"[^ng-signals-rxjs]

What Angular signals are
- Signals are a built-in reactivity primitive in Angular for representing values that change over time. A signal holds a value and notifies dependents automatically when that value changes, so code that reads the signal re-evaluates/reacts without manual subscription management[^ng-signals-overview].
- There are a few related primitives: writable signals (you can set their value), computed signals (derive a value from other signals), and effects (run imperative code in response to signal changes) — together these let you express reactive data flow in the app[^ng-signals-overview].

How they behave (short)
- Reading a signal registers a dependency; when the signal is updated, Angular re-runs computed signals and effects that depend on it.
- Signals are synchronous by default: updates propagate immediately to dependents.
- Signals interoperate with existing RxJS Observables via helpers like toSignal() and toObservable() to convert between the two forms of reactivity[^ng-signals-rxjs].

When to use signals
- Use signals when you want simpler, explicit local state and reactive derivations without the boilerplate of subscriptions and change-detection hacks. They reduce the need to manually manage subscriptions, Subjects, or manual change detection for many common patterns[^ng-signals-overview].
- Prefer signals for component-local state or derived view-model values where synchronous, fine-grained reactivity is helpful (e.g., computed values used by the template).
- Use computed signals to encapsulate derived logic instead of recomputing in templates or in getters that trigger extra change detection work.
- Use effects for side effects that should run in response to signal changes (e.g., logging, imperatively updating non-Angular APIs).
- When you already use RxJS streams across many layers, continue using Observables; convert when needed. Signals are complementary to RxJS — use toSignal/toObservable when bridging between the two models rather than rewriting everything at once[^ng-signals-rxjs][^ng-signals-overview].

Concise recommendation
- Adopt signals for component and local state that benefits from direct, synchronous dependency tracking and simpler code (computed values + effects).
- Keep using Observables where their stream semantics (time, cancellation, complex operators) are required, and bridge between the two when appropriate[^ng-signals-overview][^ng-signals-rxjs].

Sources I found:
- Angular guide: "Signals"[^ng-signals-overview]
- Angular guide: "RxJS interop with signals"[^ng-signals-rxjs]

What Angular signals are
- Signals are a built-in reactivity primitive in Angular for representing values that change over time. A signal holds a value and notifies dependents automatically when that value changes, so code that reads the signal re-evaluates/reacts without manual subscription management[^ng-signals-overview].
- There are a few related primitives: writable signals (you can set their value), computed signals (derive a value from other signals), and effects (run imperative code in response to signal changes) — together these let you express reactive data flow in the app[^ng-signals-overview].

How they behave (short)
- Reading a signal registers a dependency; when the signal is updated, Angular re-runs computed signals and effects that depend on it.
- Signals are synchronous by default: updates propagate immediately to dependents.
- Signals interoperate with existing RxJS Observables via helpers like toSignal() and toObservable() to convert between the two forms of reactivity[^ng-signals-rxjs].

When to use signals
- Use signals when you want simpler, explicit local state and reactive derivations without the boilerplate of subscriptions and change-detection hacks. They reduce the need to manually manage subscriptions, Subjects, or manual change detection for many common patterns[^ng-signals-overview].
- Prefer signals for component-local state or derived view-model values where synchronous, fine-grained reactivity is helpful (e.g., computed values used by the template).
- Use computed signals to encapsulate derived logic instead of recomputing in templates or in getters that trigger extra change detection work.
- Use effects for side effects that should run in response to signal changes (e.g., logging, imperatively updating non-Angular APIs).
- When you already use RxJS streams across many layers, continue using Observables; convert when needed. Signals are complementary to RxJS — use toSignal/toObservable when bridging between the two models rather than rewriting everything at once[^ng-signals-rxjs][^ng-signals-overview].

Concise recommendation
- Adopt signals for component and local state that benefits from direct, synchronous dependency tracking and simpler code (computed values + effects).
- Keep using Observables where their stream semantics (time, cancellation, complex operators) are required, and bridge between the two when appropriate[^ng-signals-overview][^ng-signals-rxjs].

content.text:
Sources I found:
- Angular guide: "Signals"[^ng-signals-overview]
- Angular guide: "RxJS interop with signals"[^ng-signals-rxjs]

What Angular signals are
- Signals are a built-in reactivity primitive in Angular for representing values that change over time. A signal holds a value and notifies dependents automatically when that value changes, so code that reads the signal re-evaluates/reacts without manual subscription management[^ng-signals-overview].
- There are a few related primitives: writable signals (you can set their value), computed signals (derive a value from other signals), and effects (run imperative code in response to signal changes) — together these let you express reactive data flow in the app[^ng-signals-overview].

How they behave (short)
- Reading a signal registers a dependency; when the signal is updated, Angular re-runs computed signals and effects that depend on it.
- Signals are synchronous by default: updates propagate immediately to dependents.
- Signals interoperate with existing RxJS Observables via helpers like toSignal() and toObservable() to convert between the two forms of reactivity[^ng-signals-rxjs].

When to use signals
- Use signals when you want simpler, explicit local state and reactive derivations without the boilerplate of subscriptions and change-detection hacks. They reduce the need to manually manage subscriptions, Subjects, or manual change detection for many common patterns[^ng-signals-overview].
- Prefer signals for component-local state or derived view-model values where synchronous, fine-grained reactivity is helpful (e.g., computed values used by the template).
- Use computed signals to encapsulate derived logic instead of recomputing in templates or in getters that trigger extra change detection work.
- Use effects for side effects that should run in response to signal changes (e.g., logging, imperatively updating non-Angular APIs).
- When you already use RxJS streams across many layers, continue using Observables; convert when needed. Signals are complementary to RxJS — use toSignal/toObservable when bridging between the two models rather than rewriting everything at once[^ng-signals-rxjs][^ng-signals-overview].

Concise recommendation
- Adopt signals for component and local state that benefits from direct, synchronous dependency tracking and simpler code (computed values + effects).
- Keep using Observables where their stream semantics (time, cancellation, complex operators) are required, and bridge between the two when appropriate[^ng-signals-overview][^ng-signals-rxjs].

content.text:
Sources I found:
- Angular guide: "Signals"[^ng-signals-overview]
- Angular guide: "RxJS interop with signals"[^ng-signals-rxjs]

What Angular signals are
- Signals are a built-in reactivity primitive in Angular for representing values that change over time. A signal holds a value and notifies dependents automatically when that value changes, so code that reads the signal re-evaluates/reacts without manual subscription management[^ng-signals-overview].
- There are a few related primitives: writable signals (you can set their value), computed signals (derive a value from other signals), and effects (run imperative code in response to signal changes) — together these let you express reactive data flow in the app[^ng-signals-overview].

How they behave (short)
- Reading a signal registers a dependency; when the signal is updated, Angular re-runs computed signals and effects that depend on it.
- Signals are synchronous by default: updates propagate immediately to dependents.
- Signals interoperate with existing RxJS Observables via helpers like toSignal() and toObservable() to convert between the two forms of reactivity[^ng-signals-rxjs].

When to use signals
- Use signals when you want simpler, explicit local state and reactive derivations without the boilerplate of subscriptions and change-detection hacks. They reduce the need to manually manage subscriptions, Subjects, or manual change detection for many common patterns[^ng-signals-overview].
- Prefer signals for component-local state or derived view-model values where synchronous, fine-grained reactivity is helpful (e.g., computed values used by the template).
- Use computed signals to encapsulate derived logic instead of recomputing in templates or in getters that trigger extra change detection work.
- Use effects for side effects that should run in response to signal changes (e.g., logging, imperatively updating non-Angular APIs).
- When you already use RxJS streams across many layers, continue using Observables; convert when needed. Signals are complementary to RxJS — use toSignal/toObservable when bridging between the two models rather than rewriting everything at once[^ng-signals-rxjs][^ng-signals-overview].

Concise recommendation
- Adopt signals for component and local state that benefits from direct, synchronous dependency tracking and simpler code (computed values + effects).
- Keep using Observables where their stream semantics (time, cancellation, complex operators) are required, and bridge between the two when appropriate[^ng-signals-overview][^ng-signals-rxjs].

content.text:
Sources I found:
- Angular guide: "Signals"[^ng-signals-overview]
- Angular guide: "RxJS interop with signals"[^ng-signals-rxjs]

What Angular signals are
- Signals are a built-in reactivity primitive in Angular for representing values that change over time. A signal holds a value and notifies dependents automatically when that value changes, so code that reads the signal re-evaluates/reacts without manual subscription management[^ng-signals-overview].
- There are a few related primitives: writable signals (you can set their value), computed signals (derive a value from other signals), and effects (run imperative code in response to signal changes) — together these let you express reactive data flow in the app[^ng-signals-overview].

How they behave (short)
- Reading a signal registers a dependency; when the signal is updated, Angular re-runs computed signals and effects that depend on it.
- Signals are synchronous by default: updates propagate immediately to dependents.
- Signals interoperate with existing RxJS Observables via helpers like toSignal() and toObservable() to convert between the two forms of reactivity[^ng-signals-rxjs].

When to use signals
- Use signals when you want simpler, explicit local state and reactive derivations without the boilerplate of subscriptions and change-detection hacks. They reduce the need to manually manage subscriptions, Subjects, or manual change detection for many common patterns[^ng-signals-overview].
- Prefer signals for component-local state or derived view-model values where synchronous, fine-grained reactivity is helpful (e.g., computed values used by the template).
- Use computed signals to encapsulate derived logic instead of recomputing in templates or in getters that trigger extra change detection work.
- Use effects for side effects that should run in response to signal changes (e.g., logging, imperatively updating non-Angular APIs).
- When you already use RxJS streams across many layers, continue using Observables; convert when needed. Signals are complementary to RxJS — use toSignal/toObservable when bridging between the two models rather than rewriting everything at once[^ng-signals-rxjs][^ng-signals-overview].

Concise recommendation
- Adopt signals for component and local state that benefits from direct, synchronous dependency tracking and simpler code (computed values + effects).
- Keep using Observables where their stream semantics (time, cancellation, complex operators) are required, and bridge between the two when appropriate[^ng-signals-overview][^ng-signals-rxjs].

content.text:
Sources I found:
- Angular guide: "Signals"[^ng-signals-overview]
- Angular guide: "RxJS interop with signals"[^ng-signals-rxjs]

What Angular signals are
- Signals are a built-in reactivity primitive in Angular for representing values that change over time. A signal holds a value and notifies dependents automatically when that value changes, so code that reads the signal re-evaluates/reacts without manual subscription management[^ng-signals-overview].
- There are a few related primitives: writable signals (you can set their value), computed signals (derive a value from other signals), and effects (run imperative code in response to signal changes) — together these let you express reactive data flow in the app[^ng-signals-overview].

How they behave (short)
- Reading a signal registers a dependency; when the signal is updated, Angular re-runs computed signals and effects that depend on it.
- Signals are synchronous by default: updates propagate immediately to dependents.
- Signals interoperate with existing RxJS Observables via helpers like toSignal() and toObservable() to convert between the two forms of reactivity[^ng-signals-rxjs].

When to use signals
- Use signals when you want simpler, explicit local state and reactive derivations without the boilerplate of subscriptions and change-detection hacks. They reduce the need to manually manage subscriptions, Subjects, or manual change detection for many common patterns[^ng-signals-overview].
- Prefer signals for component-local state or derived view-model values where synchronous, fine-grained reactivity is helpful (e.g., computed values used by the template).
- Use computed signals to encapsulate derived logic instead of recomputing in templates or in getters that trigger extra change detection work.
- Use effects for side effects that should run in response to signal changes (e.g., logging, imperatively updating non-Angular APIs).
- When you already use RxJS streams across many layers, continue using Observables; convert when needed. Signals are complementary to RxJS — use toSignal/toObservable when bridging between the two models rather than rewriting everything at once[^ng-signals-rxjs][^ng-signals-overview].

Concise recommendation
- Adopt signals for component and local state that benefits from direct, synchronous dependency tracking and simpler code (computed values + effects).
- Keep using Observables where their stream semantics (time, cancellation, complex operators) are required, and bridge between the two when appropriate[^ng-signals-overview][^ng-signals-rxjs].
